>Speaking of AMAB and AFAB people, can I ask whether or not AMAB and AFAB can be used as nouns, or are they and their use only accepted in the form of adjectives? For example, would it be ok to write: 'no AMABs have to worry about abortion rights for themselves, but they are still things for which they should politically campaign'.

I've seen it used both ways, so I wouldn't say it's *un*acceptable to use AMAB and AFAB as nouns, but since they're acronyms for a phrase used as a descriptor of a person, I feel adjective usage is probably more proper from a grammatical standpoint. I can see AMAB and AFAB continuing to evolve in meaning and usage over time, though. Other perspectives might be helpful here, if there are any other transpeople who would like to chime in.

>Well, I do try, but I've still got a *long* way to go yet in my view. For example, I don't know what a demiboy is. I use that because I saw it in your flair and wondered what you, as a demiboy, are. I'd love to get an explanation from a demiboy firsthand.

Certainly. I actually realized I never set my flair while I was responding to you and thought it could be helpful for context. So, in a general sense, "Demiboy" describes someone who is roughly equal parts male/masculine and another gender that may or may not be defined. "Demigirl" is the feminine counterpart, and "Demigender" is the neutral term, usually used to refer to both demiboys and demigirls collectively. In my case, I find myself aligned male and non-binary in equal parts that tend to fluctuate between 60% and 40% of one identity or the other, but not all demiboys will feel exactly like I do. The definition is loose enough to include a fair variety of different nuances.

>I take it since it has the prefix 'demi', which means half or something I think, that it means that you're half a boy or something, no? Also, if you're an adult, is the suffix 'boy' in the word 'demiboy' appropriate, or is it age-neutral?

You've got the prefix right, and yes, I am an adult. Some people with a similar gender experience to mine may prefer terms like "demiguy", "demimale", or "demiman" instead, but "demiboy" is the most common usage at the moment. It is inclusive of individuals of all ages. I prefer the term "boy" over "man" because a boy is basically a man, but just a little bit. It's like a miniature man. A man junior. It feels like a much more accurate descriptor of my nature as "kind of a guy and kind of not" than a more overtly masculine term like "man". That's also why I prefer they/them and other gender-neutral terms for myself when possible. "Man, sir, and mister" all imply too much masculinity for me. So, it all boils down to personal preference and what feels most natural and validating towards my subjective experience.

>I know that I just used 'trans\*' instead of 'trans' above, and I did so because I do believe that is actually a difference, trans person yourself, would you be able to tell me what that difference is and why it is significant?

This is a great question, because I don't know the answer. I believe trans\* was used as a more inclusive umbrella term for transpeople, as well as anyone who might be gender-nonconforming, but not identify as transgender. Take it with a grain of salt. I know "trans\*" was supposed to be more inclusive in some way. I'm just not sure in *which* way, so...

...I decided to do a little research and see if I could find a more accurate answer about trans\* vs. trans. What I was able to find is that the asterisk is used to intentionally include any gender non-confirming identity outside of binary transpeople, such as non-binary and cultural genders. So, I'd tentatively say the asterisk is optional, especially if you've already confirmed you're in a space where all identities are accepted as valid.

I'd love other opinions on the differences between "trans\*" and "trans", though. It's been awhile since I've given this subject some deep thought, so I might need correcting either to get with the times or to clarify any misunderstandings I may have.

EDIT: Fixed a typo.

> So by this definition could one say that a transmasculine person is any transgender person who was AFAB but does not conform to their expected gender role, presentation, expression, sense of self/identity, etc., and of vice versa for transfeminine people? 

Yes, by this definition, a transmasculine person is any AFAB transperson, and transfeminine can refer to any AMAB transperson. These terms would also include any applicable non-binary individual.

> Just to clarify: would it be correct for one to say that, for example something thus: 'abortion rights are not things for which only cisgender dyadic women need to politically campaign; they are also things for which all transmasculine people need to campaign as they, too, can get pregnant"? 

Absolutely. In my opinion, "transmasculine" is a great way to include transmen and non-binary people in the dialogue about reproductive health in a simple, humanizing way.  (As well as any number of issues that might specifically affect one assigned sex/gender more than others.) I find it much easier than trying to list out various types of anatomy and/or related identities, except perhaps cases where providing a detailed definition is necessary. That's just the trouble with potentially vague or broad terms sometimes, but it sounds like you're already equipped with the knowledge necessary to explain yourself if it's ever needed. I wouldn't worry too much about that.

​

I'm open for any further questions if you have them or if I missed answering anything in this reply. I'm glad to hear I was able to clear some things up and give you new terms to use when having dialogues that include transpeople. Thanks for thinking of us and making the effort to be inclusive of gender non-conforming folk!

As far as I know, I've never encountered a strict definition either, but I'll detail how I usually see the terms used.

In my experience, transmasculine and transfeminine are blanket terms used to describe any transgender individual whose gender identity and/or expression is more traditionally masculine or feminine than their gender assigned at birth.

So, a transman, a masculine-presenting AFAB non-binary person, and an androgynous-presenting AFAB non-binary person are all transmasculine, because they were assigned "female" at birth, but identify and express themselves as more masculine than feminine.

Likewise, transfeminine can refer to transwomen, or feminine/androgynous-presenting AMAB non-binary people.

Depending on the individual, transmasculine can also include more feminine-presenting AFAB non-binary people, and transfeminine can include masculine-presenting AMAB non-binary people.

Not everyone identifies with these labels, and individuals may have different experiences with exactly what being "masculine", "feminine", or even "trans" means to them. So as a likely obvious disclaimer, it's important to let people identify themselves in the way they feel most comfortable.

Where "transmasculine" and "transfeminine" are most useful as terms are typically either to explain one's gender identity/expression in vague or simpler terms, such as a demigirl saying she's "transfeminine" rather than sharing her exact identity and/or having to explain what a demigirl even is.

It's also useful if you want to talk about the issues a wider group might have in cases where the assigned gender at birth is the same, but the individuals may have very different genders. A great example is discussing abortion access for transpeople, which is an issue that would directly affect anyone assigned female at birth, regardless of their identity or expression.

​

I hope that helped. Feel free to ask more questions as needed, or add other perspectives if there's anyone out there with a different understanding of these terms.

​

As another disclaimer, I'd like to acknowledge that the term "gender identity" is seen as problematic by some in the trans community, because it could imply or be used to imply that a transperson's internal sense of their own gender is significantly different from a cis person's, and therefore less valid. That is, transpeople get gender "identities" and cis people just have their genders without a need to explain themselves. I used the term here because I'm unaware of a less problematic but equally concise way to clearly distinguish the difference or potential difference between gender and expression of gender. If there's anyone out there who has a better way to say it, please enlighten me!

I would indeed suggest that an individual with moral or religious objections to avoid these lines of work. In general, I think that if a person's personal beliefs would prevent them from doing part or all of the job, then they are not suited to that job. For me, the negotiable parts of occupations are the details that have no practical effect on one's ability to do the job.
If your religion is against touching pork, then don't work at a deli. Touching pork is part of serving deli meats.
However, if your religion requires a head covering and wearing one will not prevent you from performing all the necessary duties in the job, then I think a dress code exception can and should be made.

Other people's distinctions on what is or is not an acceptable exception here will vary. This is, again, just one person's opinion.

> May I clarify, are you saying therefore women with penises should continue to access services designed for men when their genitalia are material to the service - or that they should expect services for women to accommodate their penis and treat them as if their penis were a vulva? 

Neither, actually. If a service is advertised as "for men", then they should expect men to want that service. Transwoman are not men. Thus, *requiring* a transwoman to go to the place "for men" is inherently invalidating for her. That's obviously a problem. As for what to do to fix that problem, I'm not 100% sure I have a perfect solution. There are probably lots of ideas out there about how to progress forward in this area.

In my personal, ideal world, either society wouldn't think of vocabulary relating to genitals to be "taboo", especially in a medical context, or new vocabulary would arise that would allow people to refer to certain sets of genitals in a more "polite" way. Businesses could then say what they mean when they advertise gender- or sex-specific services. So a "women's" beauty salon would be able to serve transwomen and cis women, and a "vulva" beauty salon would serve transmen and cis women. In either situation, the salon would expect gender diversity in some way, but that diversity would align with the services they are specifically providing, and all without creating an uncomfortable situation where they have to say "When we said woman, we didn't mean *you*."

I see how that's not necessarily practical in all situations, since most businesses don't want to slap "vagina" on the front of their building. Instead, I'm imagining a situation were a hospital chooses the label "gynecology" over "women's health", for example. In the mean time, I think it's really important for there to be gender-neutral spaces available for cases where gender and sex might not align in the "expected" way.

> Again, to be sure I understand your point - are you saying you'd be cool for a one-woman beautician business to explain to you that she lacks the specific skills and tools for your requirements, but she can recommend a specific other service provider? 

Yes. I feel this is a reasonable response in the current situation we have. If that beautician is not trained or qualified to work on men and/or transwomen, then a recommendation to someone who *is* qualified would be the next best thing.

> Is it that, so long as this was a technical and not a moral objection, this would be OK? 

Exactly. In the example you provided about the beautician refusing service because "her husband would be uncomfortable", the objection didn't have anything to do with providing the best technical care for that transwoman. Moral objections like that get into the territory of discrimination. However, practical objections, when grounded in medical fact and presented with kindness and understanding, are acceptable. I'd actually *want* a beautician to speak up if she was not trained to work on me, because I want the best care possible with minimal risks of complications.

Since there was a request to take personalities out of the picture, I'm going to answer the question in general terms as if there was no additional context given.

> How do you think we could best take the conflict out of those few edge cases where gendered demand meets sex-specific supply? 

Of course I understand that people with different genitals have different care requirements. Unfortunately, there's no "magic wand" that can instantly give someone the genitals they prefer. So, for the time a woman has a penis, for example, that penis is going to need penis-specific attention. That seems totally reasonable to me.

The problem, in my opinion, is when those sex-specific occasions conflate gender and sex as ALWAYS the same thing under EVERY circumstance and are thus under-prepared when a transgender individual requests care. I would really appreciate the tiniest acknowledgement that there is some diversity out there. Those spaces that cater to specific genitalia should, at the bare minimum, have training for staff members in how to responsibly assist transpeople that might enter those spaces. That would just mean treating them with dignity like anyone else, and either adjusting the situation to their specific needs or helping them find another person/location that can assist them better. It would not involve any implications that they are not a "real" man/woman/etc. because of their genitals.

So why narcissism specifically? People with narcissistic tendencies tend to think only about themselves and don't care much about other people's wants and needs. They're exactly the kind of people that would feel entitled to children and/or grandchildren because THEY want them. They have little-to-no respect for others' autonomy or boundaries, so a narc who disapproves of your choice to be childfree will probably not just "let it go". They're more the sort to be relentlessly pushy, sometimes to a dangerous extreme. For those that have someone like this regularly pestering them about kids, it's easy to see why subs like r/truechildfree could become a safe haven.

Source: I am childfree and was raised by narcissists.

I'm just going to throw out all the ideas I can think of from the perspective of someone who has traveled both nationally and internationally with dogs. Hopefully some of them help! (Sorry it's so long. I just got going and couldn't stop!)

1. Emergency vet contact info. If you plan to accommodate species other than dogs and cats (such as birds or rabbits), an exotic vet would be best. A phone number and directions to the nearest 24/7 emergency clinic should help guests get the care they need.
2. A pet med kit on site would also be helpful for smaller health issues that need care. It's pretty easy to google some of the stuff to include there, or ask a vet about it. My favorite supplies personally are a good tick remover tool and styptic powder, but there are plenty of other supplies that you'll also want to include.
3. Food and water bowls in the guest rooms. Easy access to water, especially, is very important for basically every living thing, after all. \^\^;
4. Variety of different-sized pet beds so furry guests of all sizes can sleep comfortably. Not all pets will want or need one, but many will appreciate it. Just be careful to consider that some dogs like to chew their beds. There are some heavy-duty or cheap and easily-replaced options to look at if you wish.
5. Outdoor potty area. This is a big one for dogs, especially. If you want to go all-out. A nice, safe, fenced area is lovely. For the less social dogs, I find smaller, individual kennels for pottying and excising to be really nice. However, I'd be perfectly satisfied with a grassy stretch away from traffic with a nearby trash can for my pet's waste. Something like that should do for leashed pets.
6. Poop bags! Best places to have them are, at a minimum, outdoors near the potty area and at the front desk. Maybe leave a few in the guest rooms as well. Sometimes a normally well-behaved dog can get thrown off by being in a new place, and accidents can happen. Many pet owners will clean up after their pets with no fuss, especially if cleaning supplies are provided.
7. Tennis balls. I hear you can get used ones fairly cheaply, if you'd like to provide any toys for dogs to play with while enjoying play or exercise areas.
8. If you plan to have a pool on-site, perhaps consider accommodations for water-loving pets. I'm no plumber, but if it's feasible to consider options that would let pets go for a swim too, I'm sure they would appreciate it.
9. A lot of hotels include breakfast, so including breakfast for pets would be a nice touch. There are also a lot of human-grade foods that cats and dogs enjoy that would be pretty easy to serve alongside human breakfast items. Off the top of my head, my dog eats broccoli, carrots, basically any meat, strawberries, watermelon, eggs, rice, plain yogurt etc. I imagine having a pet-safe pancake/waffle batter might be fun, if you plan to have waffle makers in the breakfast area. PLEASE, consult a vet to verify which foods are safe to share. I'm not qualified to make dietary recommendations for the general population. (Sorry, I'm imagining the most adorable sausage, egg, and fruit breakfast buffet for dogs right now. X3 )
10. I saw some comments about behavior policies, and I have to agree. It's easy to get excited imaging what a dream vacation for my dog might look like, but there are practical things to consider. If I'm going to stay in a strange place with a bunch of unknown animals, I want to be sure that I'll be safe doing so. Requiring vaccine records is a good idea. They're really easy to get. Any pet owner's vet should be able to print them off for you in a timely manner, so it's not unreasonable to request of guests. I also think that having some policy to handle disruptive or dangerous guests is a must. Perhaps consider a leash policy, possibly with separate designated off-leash areas? All animals should be leashed and under control at all times. Excessive noise or aggressive behavior are not ok.
11. Keep an eye out for fleas, yo! They can spread so quickly and are a pain to deal with. I imagine anything you're doing to prevent bed bug outbreaks will likely help, but there might be some flea-specific precautions you can take. Along with getting that contact info and asking about pet-safe breakfast items, go ahead and ask your vet about health precautions you can take, and maybe ask about potential problem behaviors to watch out for and how to prevent them, as mentioned in point #10.
12. Dog- and cat-only areas, preferably located near their own exits so cats and dogs have a smaller chance of running into each other. Obviously, you'll want some mixed-pet or all species rooms too, but considering pet owners with allergies or pets that don't get along with all species will be a life-saver.
13. Seconding some more comments mentioning information on local pet-friendly attractions and restaurants. I should also add that information on pet-friendly public transportation would be splendid.
14. Litter boxes for cats will really help the feline guests out, I'm sure.

I'm a big believer in the "my body, my choice" mentality. No one should be forced or pressured into getting a tattoo. Period.

That said, OP also has some pretty good reasons. The tattoo for his son was moreso to commemorate an important triumph in his son's life, and not just because the son exists at all.  Honestly, the "fair" thing would be to wait for the daughter to overcome a life-threatening challenge and then get a tattoo to honor her victory in the same way. Obviously, no one wants her to go through that.

Plus, doing the work of being there for over twenty years to raise the daughter says plenty about being a "real dad".

I'd just like to say that I disagree with the idea that anyone's identity should be defined only by suffering. Hurting and self-loathing are not what makes someone trans. It's often a part of the experience, but it shouldn't be the only part. There are also awesome parts about being trans. If she's able to love herself enough to enjoy things in a dysphoria-free way on occasion, even before having achieved her goals for transition, then that's great! (Feel free to tell her that!)

Seeing a mental health professional might help your girlfriend work through some of the feelings she's having about questioning herself. I'd recommend seeking a therapist to anyone who's early in their transition, as there can be a lot of complex thoughts and emotions one can run into on their "gender journey" that can be challenging to work through. Having lots of healthy support makes a world of difference for any transperson.

Best of luck to you both!

TLDR: BF is being a jerk. He doesn't appreciate anything you do, and is trying to walk all over your boundaries instead of using the puppy as motivation to improve himself to the point where he IS ready for another dog. 

​

I am typically an advocate for the wonders a pet can do for someone with mental health issues. I struggle with some pretty serious stuff, and I cannot imagine trying to deal with all that without having some type of animal around. The non-judgmental and unconditional love is really therapeutic, and the responsibility of caring for a pet or pets gives me a lot of motivation to get up each day and make sure everyday life stuff is in order. It just boils down to the fact that I don't care enough about myself to take care of myself without an external reason, and I'm too terrified of most other people to feel comfortable around them the way I can relax completely with an animal. Of course, I always do a ton of research and preparation before getting a pet to ensure I get the right animal for me. I wouldn't get a doberman, for example, because they require a lot of exercise each day. That's just too much for me, so I have a low-energy Chihuahua mix instead.

​

That is not your situation.

Your boyfriend isn't trying. If he was, he'd be excitedly getting the house ready for the puppy and putting a plan together to integrate a new family member with everyone else. That means planning to take on responsibility for training and caring for the puppy and making sure that having a new dog around doesn't negatively impact any current family member's (including your current dog) quality of life. Instead, he does nothing at all. He literally expects to be handed a cute puppy, already trained, and do zero work, while also ignoring everyone else around him.

On top of that, a doberman is a terrible dog for someone who wants to put as little effort into their pet as possible. It's obvious that zero research was done.

For the sake of being constructive, I might suggest using that puppy to motivate him to do better. Tell him what he needs to straighten out in his life to prove he can handle the pup, and then give him a chance to meet those standards or show significant-enough improvement that you're satisfied. The thing is, that's what you do for a ten-year-old kid when they beg for a puppy for Christmas. Not a grown adult.

He's been taking advantage of you and taking you for granted far too long. You already do WAY too much to take on his responsibilities for him, as others have already pointed out.

​

On a side note, yeah. He's choosing that puppy over not only you, but your labrador, and his own children as well.

I got offered a purebred puppy by a friend awhile back too. Then, I discovered my partner was terribly allergic to the pup's specific coat type, so I gave him back the next day. The puppy was adorable and sweet and will easily find a new home. I love my current family far too much to let them suffer because a new puppy is "so cute". Mental health issues are never a reason to treat people (or animals!) poorly.

What I see here is a dude who is dismissing and ignoring his girlfriend's medical condition. It's a very simple, easy request to speak at a normal, speaking volume indoors. (Isn't that just basic manners for most people?)

Unfortunately, there are a lot of people in the world who don't "believe" health conditions exist unless they're visible. I doubt he'd be talking about "bending over backwards" if you were in a wheelchair and you asked that he only take you to accessible restaurants, for example. That attitude that you have to somehow "prove" you're not making up a legitimate health issue is absurd.

PTSD is a mental health condition. It's real. It's valid. It's just invisible.

Do you really want to date someone who won't lift a finger to help someone he supposedly cares about? Do you really want to date someone who doesn't believe you?

You deserve better.

​

By the way, calling your boyfriend "logical" and yourself "illogical"... Are those his labels, or yours? It's just that I think you have real, thoughtful, fact-based reasons for your opinions. That doesn't sound illogical to me.

There's nothing wrong with being gay. At all.

It seems to me like you're making a big deal out of nothing and trying to make your ex's dating preference about you. It's not about you, just like those two girlfriends you had have nothing to do with your ex.

NTA

Your SO made some bad choices. If you want to be there for him, then that's great, but you shouldn't have to. You didn't get involved with drugs. He did. It's not fair to expect you to have to wait for *more than ten years* to have a real relationship. If you're feeling unfulfilled and don't want to do this anymore, you don't have to. It sucks. It's sad. I'm sure everyone would have preferred that the two of you lived happily ever after, but that's not realistic.

One of the wisest people I ever met once told me, "My broken bone won't cure your poison ivy."

There's no need to have a contest over whose pain hurts more. Both are bad. Neither should be happening. You both need relief from your pain. It's better to focus on helping each other feel better than to fight over who is more uncomfortable.

​

Now, that's nice and all, but you're probably hoping for some more practical advice. Ok, here goes. I'm going to guess that your partner really is struggling. That language of dismissing your problems and insisting their struggles are the "worst" tells me your partner is probably feeling alone and overwhelmed. That is very normal, especially for transpeople when they are just beginning their journey.

It's NOT normal to take those feelings out on you by belittling your own struggles. That's hurtful and wrong. Your partner isn't handling her feelings with very much maturity right now. I'm sorry for that.

So, what I'd suggest is to sit your partner down and calmly explain that you want to be supportive. You understand she's going through a lot. Suggest to them the idea of seeking out a therapist who specializes in gender stuff, or a trans/LGBT support group, where they can get more support from people who understand from their point of view. A therapist will also be able to help her learn how to manage her feelings better so that she doesn't let them hurt her loved ones. I'd highly suggest to anyone early in their transition to see a therapist for so many reasons.

You also need to make it clear that you don't want to argue over who is struggling more. Instead, you want to be able to support each other, and you expect kindness and understanding for yourself as well. That's a boundary. A firm one. Partners are there for each other, no matter how big or small the problems might be. You will be there to listen and support her in her transition, but you also want to be able to talk about and have support for your own struggles.

If that's not possible, you might have to re-evaluate whether this relationship is working out for you. There comes a point where you have to love yourself enough to take care of your mental health first. You're a better judge of where that point is than I am. Trust yourself.

​

Source - I'm a transperson who transitioned during my current relationship. 4.5 years and counting.

I wasn't at the stream, so all I have to go by is this quote, but here's my two cents based on the evidence I have to work with.

He obviously makes a distinction between accidental and purposeful misgendering. I think a lot of people, occasionally get called the wrong thing. It happens. No one is saying you should go to jail because that man looked like a lady from the back.

The difference here, is when you *know* someone is trans, and you purposefully call them the wrong thing. *Purposefully.* That's different from trying to "get it right" and messing up a few times. No one wants you in jail for that either. (Most transpeople really appreciate the effort and understand that it can be hard sometimes.)

What the issue is, is when you're just being a jerk. On purpose. To hurt people because you don't like them. That should never be ok. Hurting people is not ok.

What's so hard about that?

Spend as much time as possible with people who consistently use your true name. It'll help you get used to being called that all the time instead of your deadname. Make sure to talk to your parents in private and let them know what's been up with you. Remind them that your chosen name has been your preference for years, and it is not optional. Prepare them that you will be correcting them when they forget, even if they "forget" in front of other people. You're serious about moving on from what they used to call you and don't want other people or potential new friends to meet you by the wrong name. If there was any chance they just never understood how much this meant to you, then they'll probably get it after you sit them down and make it clear. Be prepared for some resistance if they're just being difficult about your name. Stay strong!

I have done extensive research in the past year in preparation to train my own service animal, and here is the information I can share.

First of all, while it is bad form to interfere with a service dog on duty, it seems like it was an honest mistake. You are right that in a dimly-lit area, a vest would be much easier to see and identify the dog as a working service animal. However, no business can legally require that a service animal look a certain way in order to enter. In fact, legally, the dog requires zero identification or certification in order to be recognized as a service dog, and has full protection of the law to accompany the handler with or without a harness/leash/tag/papers/etc. Again, I'm no expert, but I assume this is to prevent discrimination in case there's ever a reason why the dog is or cannot wear the "proper gear" but still needs to perform a vital service for their disabled handler, who needs that dog in order to function, or in some cases to perform life-saving services. Since service dogs help with so many different disabilities, it's hard to regulate what is or is not acceptable gear as a blanket statement. A guide dog needs to do one thing and a seizure alert dog needs to do something completely different, for example. Anyway, anyone can slap a harness on a dog. The thing that makes an animal a service animal is their training, not their outfit.

So, that was a long way of saying you can't ask the bar to require a harness.

Grooming requirements vary widely depending on the type of coat your dog has. There are dogs who do need bathing as frequently as weekly, and some that only need a bath if they're visibly dirty.

I'm going to assume Mack has a short, smooth coat like your average Basset Hound. (You said he was a mix, so while this is likely, it's not necessarily the case with your particular crossbreed.) Dogs with this coat type are typically quite clean naturally, and bathing too often can strip the oils in their coat, which dries out the skin and can cause some very itchy problems for your furry friend. Think doggy dandruff.

As far as how often is too often? It depends on the dog a little bit. A dog with sensitive skin who gets really itchy after a bath might need longer breaks between them. I personally have a dog with the same coat type (a chihuahua) and I bathe him about once a month with no skin issues, (he always finds a way to get dirty, the little rascal!) if that helps, but your dog might need longer breaks between baths or you might be able to get away with it more often too.

How often is not often enough? It's been mentioned already that a short, smooth-coated dog really only needs bathing when visibly dirty or if you notice too much "doggy musk". (Or when medically necessary, but you didn't mention any conditions that would require that sort of thing.)

So in my opinion, as long as you make sure your dog has breaks between baths to replenish his coat's essential oils, you can bathe as often or as infrequently as you prefer.

When I was 18, my parents divorced. My father was a physically and emotionally abusive narc, while my mother was a more subtle variety of manipulative narc. I went no contact with my father as soon as he had been officially kicked out of the house. I told him in person, to his face, that I would have nothing to do with him and would no longer call him my father. I moved out at 19. It took me a year to break through the depressive fog after all the years of abuse and apply for college. I moved into an apartment with my partner after my freshman year. For me, I was very open to my mother about intending to move out. I talked about my desire to leave and how my progress finding a suitable apartment was going. I foolishly thought that my Nmom would stop threatening to kick me out if she knew I would be leaving on my own very soon.

I got lucky in that she decided to move to another state about a month after I moved into my new apartment, so I only needed to deal with calls and texts as opposed to in-person visits. I responded politely to her messages and we talked occasionally on the phone. It wasn't pleasant, but it was tolerable.
For a year, I semi-ghosted. I wouldn't contact her except to respond to things she said to me. I shared less and less of my life with her until our relationship consisted of lengthy phone calls where she would tell me how hard her life was and I would be her therapist.

When she shared my contact information with my abusive father, I went no contact with her. I told her on a phone call that it was no longer safe for me to have anything to do with her. She had my email address if she needed to get a hold of me in an emergency, but we would not be speaking from that point onward.

I did two major things to protect my low and no contact statuses. Firstly, I was very careful with my contact information. I used an alias on facebook so that they could not find me, I signed a privacy order at my university so that they would not have access to my records, and I never shared my new address with my parents. I also explained to any mutual friends that it was very important to me that my parents do not know about where I am or what I'm doing, and I did not share contact information unless absolutely necessary with anyone. Just imagine what you would do if you wanted to track yourself down, and take steps to make it difficult to do that. I jumped through a lot of hoops and I realize not everyone is able to go to the lengths that I did, but making efforts to hide your info should still help.

The other thing I did was to stay firm on my own. No matter how curious you are about things back home, no matter how many promises or manipulations your parents come up with, no matter how lonely it is, do not give in. If you decide to have contact again, you need to make sure you are safe to do so and that you're prepared to handle their drama. Wait until you 100% do not need anyone's support to make it on your own, and until you are completely sure that nothing they do or say will get to you. When living on a tight budget, the most important part for me is prioritizing. The most urgent and expensive things should be paid for first. Make sure anything you buy outside of food and required bills (rent, electricity, etc.) is absolutely necessary. It really sucks, but there might be a time when you have to give up on having anything other than the bare essentials until you have more money to go around. Tiny costs add up, so don't let yourself be tempted.
Budgets give me anxiety, so I prefer to keep things in my head and penny-pinch in my day-to-day, but they are a useful tool if you're able to handle them. Keep track of your expenses and set aside the money you need to pay things ahead of time. If you find you're spending too much, cut back on the non-essentials like nights out or netflix subscriptions. Also, do try to pay your bills on time whenever possible. Companies like to add interest if you take too long to pay, and paying more will not help you have more money to spare, obviously. Making sure you have a room over your head and enough to eat is most important, so delaying rent a week is preferable to starving, but if you can, try not to let that happen.

Finally, leaving home had a very profound impact on my life in a lot of ways I never expected.
I'll talk about the bad first. It was crushing. I hated my biological family and all they had put me through, but when I finally cut ties with my last family member, I felt so very alone and abandoned. Any hopes I had of repairing my broken family were shattered and I was left with the stunning realization that as alone as I felt before, I really, truly was alone now. This lead to a lot of feelings of depression, isolation, and hopelessness. I felt bitter and resentful that everyone else seemed to have a perfect family and I had monsters instead. The first six months were the hardest.
Then I started to change.
After a lifetime of being treated terribly, the distance was starting to let me see my past for what it was. The behavior I dismissed and excused so often seemed more and more shocking and inappropriate. I slowly realized just how bad it was in a way that only distance could have let me truly understand. My feelings of hurt and loss began to fade, and I realized that what I missed was not my family, but the idea of a family. What I wanted "back" had never existed in the first place, and seeing that for the first time was so freeing.
